summary: Nadab and Abihu offer fire that God had not commanded, and fire from Yahweh kills them at the sanctuary. Aaron and his remaining sons must continue their priestly service while Israel mourns; they are charged to distinguish holy from common and clean from unclean. The chapter closes not with another death but with Moses accepting Aaron’s explanation for not eating the sin offering after the family’s catastrophe.
whyItMatters: The first day of priestly service becomes a warning that access to the sanctuary is not casual. Yet the ending also shows priestly discernment working through grief, argument, and a judgment Moses is willing to reconsider.

context.author: The text presents these instructions as Yahweh’s words through Moses; authorship and final composition are debated
context.audience: Aaron, his sons, and the children of Israel, with special duties assigned to the priests
context.date: The narrative is set in Israel’s wilderness period; the date of the book’s final composition is debated
context.setting: At the Tent of Meeting, immediately after Aaron and his sons begin their priestly ministry
context.literaryForm: Priestly narrative followed by sanctuary instruction

outline.heading: Unauthorized fire and death before Yahweh
outline.note: Nadab and Abihu bring what was not commanded; Aaron responds to Moses’ explanation with silence.

outline.heading: Burial and constrained mourning
outline.note: Relatives carry the bodies outside the camp while the anointed priests remain at the Tent.

outline.heading: Sobriety, distinction, and teaching
outline.note: Yahweh directly charges Aaron and his sons to serve soberly, distinguish ritual categories, and teach Israel.

outline.heading: The priests’ assigned portions
outline.note: Moses tells the survivors where and with whom the meal and peace-offering portions may be eaten.

outline.heading: Moses and Aaron dispute the uneaten goat
outline.note: Aaron explains why eating the offering on this day would not have seemed pleasing, and Moses accepts his answer.

keyVerses.text: Then Moses said to Aaron, “This is what Yahweh spoke of, saying, ‘I will show myself holy to those who come near me, and before all the people I will be glorified.’” Aaron held his peace.
keyVerses.why: The verse states the chapter’s sanctuary principle and records Aaron’s silence after his sons’ deaths without explaining his inner response.

keyVerses.text: You are to make a distinction between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean.
keyVerses.why: The priests’ duty includes distinguishing holy from common and unclean from clean.

keyVerses.text: Aaron spoke to Moses, “Behold, today they have offered their sin offering and their burnt offering before Yahweh; and such things as these have happened to me. If I had eaten the sin offering today, would it have been pleasing in Yahweh’s sight?”
keyVerses.why: Aaron does not deny the rule; he asks how faithful service should account for what has happened that day.

questions.question: What was the “strange fire” that Nadab and Abihu offered?
questions.answer: The chapter defines it only as fire “which he had not commanded them.” It does not identify the fuel, incense mixture, source of the flame, or motive, so any more precise reconstruction goes beyond the account.

questions.question: Why are Nadab and Abihu killed for this act?
questions.answer: They approach Yahweh with an offering he had not commanded, at the beginning of the priesthood’s sanctuary work. Moses interprets the deaths through God’s holiness before those who come near. The narrative does not further explain the severity of the penalty, which remains disturbing.

questions.question: Does Aaron’s silence mean that he agrees with Moses?
questions.answer: Verse 3 says only that Aaron held his peace. In context he has just lost two sons and is still responsible for the sanctuary; the silence may convey grief, restraint, submission, or several of these at once, but the text does not label his inner response.

questions.question: Why may Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar not perform the ordinary signs of mourning?
questions.answer: Moses says that the anointing oil is on them and orders them not to leave the Tent of Meeting, while the wider house of Israel mourns. Their restriction arises from their current priestly office; it does not mean the deaths are painless or that Israel is forbidden to grieve.

questions.question: Does the warning about wine prove that Nadab and Abihu were drunk?
questions.answer: No. The command follows their deaths and clearly requires priests to avoid wine and strong drink when entering the Tent, but the chapter never says the two men had been drinking. The placement may invite readers to connect sobriety with sound judgment without supplying a cause the narrative withholds.

questions.question: What do “holy,” “common,” “unclean,” and “clean” mean here?
questions.answer: They are distinctions priests must recognize and teach for Israel’s worship. “Holy” marks what is set apart for God, while clean and unclean govern fitness for sacred contact; uncleanness in this system is not automatically a moral offense or a statement about someone’s worth.

questions.question: Why does Moses review the food portions with the surviving priests?
questions.answer: Even after the deaths, the offerings have assigned portions and places for eating. Moses distinguishes the most holy meal offering, eaten beside the altar, from the breast and thigh that sons and daughters may share in a clean place, keeping the day’s service within its stated rules.

questions.question: Why does Moses accept Aaron’s explanation about the burned goat?
questions.answer: Moses first argues that the priests should have eaten the goat because its blood had not entered the inner sanctuary. Aaron answers that, after the day’s offerings and family deaths, eating it would not have seemed pleasing to Yahweh; verse 20 records that this reasoning satisfied Moses.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: Aaron’s first public service ends with divine fire consuming the altar offering as the people shout and fall on their faces.

here.text: Fire consumes Nadab and Abihu after an unauthorized offering. The survivors receive limits on mourning and drink, duties of distinction and teaching, and instructions on priestly portions; Aaron’s explanation for leaving one goat uneaten satisfies Moses.

after.text: The command to distinguish clean from unclean and to teach Israel leads into detailed rules about food animals, carcass contact, and holiness.
